notYet: Not yet part of the western Mediterranean

stages.name: Open
stages.desc: Not named in the treaties: Roman ships may sail and trade freely

stages.name: Greek
stages.desc: Greek cities and their hinterland, outside both treaty spheres

stages.name: Roman/Latin sphere
stages.desc: Rome and the Latin towns Carthage swears not to harm

stages.name: Carthaginian-controlled
stages.desc: Carthage's own ground: Romans may trade, under the treaty's rules

stages.name: Closed to Roman ships
stages.desc: No Roman may trade, plunder or found a city here

states.name: France
timeline: Massalia (Marseille), founded by Greeks from Phocaea around 600 BC, controls the coast of Gaul
Massalia stays outside both spheres; it is long a friend of Rome

states.name: Spain
timeline: Not named in the first treaty. Phoenician Gadir (Cádiz) trades with Iberian Tartessos; Greeks trade from Emporion
Second treaty: Romans may not plunder, trade or found cities beyond Mastia of the Tarseians, in south-eastern Spain

states.name: Libya
timeline: The Emporia and the Syrtis coast lie beyond the Fair Promontory: closed to Roman ships, on Polybius's reading of the first treaty
Second treaty: no Roman may trade or found a city anywhere in Africa

states.name: Tunisia
timeline: Carthage: Roman ships may not sail beyond the Fair Promontory, north of the city, unless driven by storm or enemies; deals must be made before a herald or a clerk
Second treaty: in Carthage itself Romans may trade as freely as a citizen, though the rest of Africa is closed to them
Agathocles of Syracuse lands at Cap Bon and ravages Carthaginian Africa for three years
Carthage's garrison is expelled from Messana; war with Rome begins

states.name: Italy
timeline: First treaty: Carthage swears not to harm Ardea, Antium, Laurentum, Circeii, Tarracina or any Latin town. Rome rules only part of Latium; Sardinia and western Sicily are Carthaginian
Second treaty: Carthage may keep plunder and captives taken from Latin towns outside Roman rule, but must hand the towns themselves to Rome
Rome dissolves the Latin League and annexes much of Latium
Third treaty (Livy). Philinus later claimed a clause keeping Carthaginians out of all Italy and Romans out of all Sicily
Fourth treaty: Rome and Carthage allied against Pyrrhus, who is fighting in southern Italy
Tarentum surrenders: Rome now controls the peninsula south of the Po valley
Rome sends an army across the Strait of Messina into Sicily: the First Punic War begins

states.name: Algeria
timeline: Carthaginian Africa: Roman traders may sell here only before a herald or a clerk, and the state guarantees the price
Second treaty: Africa is closed; Romans may land only for supplies or repairs and must leave within five days

states.name: Malta
timeline: Phoenician Malta, part of Carthage's island network; not named in the treaties
Malta remains Carthaginian as war begins; Rome raids it in 257

events.title: The first treaty
events.text: In the consulship of Lucius Junius Brutus and Marcus Horatius, Rome and Carthage swear their first treaty, Polybius says.

events.title: Temple of Jupiter
events.text: Tradition says Marcus Horatius dedicates the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol, where the treaties will be kept.

events.title: The Fair Promontory
events.text: Roman ships may not sail past the headland north of Carthage unless driven by storm or enemies.

events.title: The Pyrgi tablets
events.text: Gold tablets in Etruscan and Phoenician record a ruler of Caere dedicating a shrine to Astarte.

events.title: Battle of Himera
events.text: Gelon of Syracuse and Theron of Akragas destroy a Carthaginian army in Sicily.

events.title: Battle of Cumae
events.text: Hiero of Syracuse defeats the Etruscan fleet off Campania.

events.title: Selinus destroyed
events.text: A Carthaginian army sacks Selinus and Himera; thousands are killed or enslaved.

events.title: Akragas falls
events.text: Carthage takes Akragas, one of the richest Greek cities in Sicily.

events.title: Peace with Dionysius
events.text: Dionysius of Syracuse recognises Carthage's rule over western Sicily.

events.title: Motya stormed
events.text: Dionysius takes the Phoenician island city of Motya; Carthage moves to Lilybaeum.

events.title: Gauls sack Rome
events.text: After the battle of the Allia, Gauls capture and burn most of Rome.

events.title: Pyrgi plundered
events.text: Dionysius raids Pyrgi, the port of Caere, and strips its temple.

events.title: The second treaty
events.text: Carthaginian envoys renew the treaty in Rome, now in the name of Tyre and Utica too.

events.title: Mastia
events.text: Romans may not trade, plunder or found cities beyond Mastia, near Cartagena.

events.title: Sardinia closed
events.text: Romans are barred from trading or founding cities in Sardinia.

events.title: Utica
events.text: Carthage's older sister city is named as a party to the second treaty.

events.title: A golden crown
events.text: Carthage sends a crown of twenty-five pounds of gold to Jupiter's temple to honour Rome's victories.

events.title: Battle of Crimisus
events.text: Timoleon of Corinth routs a Carthaginian army in western Sicily.

events.title: Beaks of Antium
events.text: Rome crushes the Latins and sets the prows of Antium's warships in the Forum.

events.title: Naples allies
events.text: Greek Neapolis allies with Rome as the Second Samnite War begins.

events.title: Caudine Forks
events.text: A trapped Roman army surrenders to the Samnites and passes under the yoke.

events.title: Appian Way
events.text: Appius Claudius begins the road from Rome to Capua.

events.title: Agathocles in Africa
events.text: The tyrant of Syracuse lands near Cap Bon, burns his ships and marches on Carthage.

events.title: Agathocles leaves
events.text: Defeated, Agathocles abandons his army in Africa and slips back to Sicily.

events.title: The third treaty
events.text: Livy records that the treaty with Carthage is renewed for the third time.

events.title: Philinus's claim
events.text: Philinus of Akragas later says a treaty kept Romans out of Sicily and Carthaginians out of Italy.

events.title: Battle of Sentinum
events.text: Rome defeats an alliance of Samnites and Gauls in central Italy.

events.title: Mamertines take Messana
events.text: Campanian mercenaries seize Messana, kill its men and call themselves sons of Mars.

events.title: Ships sunk at Tarentum
events.text: Tarentum attacks a Roman squadron in its gulf and calls in Pyrrhus.

events.title: Battle of Heraclea
events.text: Pyrrhus and his elephants defeat the Roman legions.

events.title: Battle of Asculum
events.text: Pyrrhus wins again at a terrible cost: the original Pyrrhic victory.

events.title: Mago at Ostia
events.text: A Carthaginian admiral arrives with over a hundred ships to offer help; the Senate declines.

events.title: The fourth treaty
events.text: Rome and Carthage ally against Pyrrhus; Carthage will supply the ships.

events.title: Pyrrhus in Sicily
events.text: Pyrrhus crosses to Sicily at the call of Syracuse.

events.title: Eryx stormed
events.text: Pyrrhus takes the Carthaginian mountain fortress of Eryx.

events.title: Lilybaeum holds
events.text: Pyrrhus fails to take Lilybaeum and leaves Sicily to Carthage and Rome.

events.title: Beneventum
events.text: Pyrrhus fights his last battle in Italy and sails home to Epirus.

events.title: Tarentum surrenders
events.text: Tarentum falls to Rome; a Carthaginian fleet offshore raises cries of a broken treaty.

events.title: Rhegium retaken
events.text: Rome retakes Rhegium from its own rebel garrison, across the strait from Messana.

events.title: Battle of Longanus
events.text: Hiero of Syracuse defeats the Mamertines, who turn to Carthage and Rome.

events.title: Rome crosses
events.text: Appius Claudius Caudex leads a Roman army across the strait to Messana.

chartNote: Share of the area of today's Italy, Tunisia, Spain, France, Malta, Algeria and Libya, coloured by what the treaties of the day meant for a Roman ship. Regions are today's boundaries and each country takes one colour, a simplification: Italy also held Carthaginian Sardinia and western Sicily and the Greek cities of the south, and the vast deserts of Algeria and Libya, never under Carthage, swing the shares. The treaties' places are debated: the Fair Promontory may be Cape Farina or Cap Bon, and Mastia lies near Cartagena.
